## Chosen hook

Calm plain opener, feeling-first rather than punchy, per the Facebook format. It opens on the object rather than on a claim, and it puts the reader in the room with his own sheet.

"One line on your results has a little flag beside it, and now it's the only line you can see."

Archetype: Teacher. No wedge and no scroll-stop: the Facebook reader is older, patient and clinical-curious, and the job is education that stands on its own value.

## Script

**Funnel:** MOFU (Capture) | job: reading-literacy explainer for the older segment | cta: quiz | format: facebook-post | marker: none
**Emotion:** Recognition, then relief. Nothing here asks him to feel worried, and nothing tells him not to act.

POST

> One line on your results has a little flag beside it, and now it's the only line you can see.
>
> Two things don't wait. Anything the lab has flagged as needing urgent attention: follow what the lab or NHS 111 tells you, promptly. And any result alongside unexplained weight loss, night sweats, a persistent fever, or blood where it shouldn't be: that's your GP, urgently, whatever the number says.
>
> That's the urgent list, and it's short.
>
> A single result is a snapshot. It names a value on a day. It doesn't name the reason, and it isn't a verdict.
>
> One number sitting outside the range on one day is often just noise. A recent cold. A hard training week. A night of bad sleep. Dehydration, the time the blood was drawn, the meal before it: any of those can nudge a marker without your baseline having moved at all.
>
> The range is drawn to cover about 19 in 20 healthy people, which by definition leaves 1 in 20 perfectly healthy people sitting outside it.
>
> A doctor doesn't read a result on its own either. They read it inside a picture: your symptoms, your history, the other markers, sometimes a retest. That's the same way to read your own.
>
> A number outside the range is a prompt to look closer. It isn't a label, and nobody should be reading a disease off a single sheet.
>
> Which puts one question ahead of the reading. What else was going on in the week you gave that sample?
>
> A snapshot is worth more when there's something to read it against. This walks through which check measures what, in a couple of minutes: https://andro-prime.com/test-selector?utm_source=facebook

## Craft notes

- **Structure chosen on avatar fit, and that is the axis it was ranked on.** Two other sections of the article were viable as standalone Facebook posts. The units section was rejected on the same ground the LinkedIn sibling rejected it: its implicit ask is "go away and learn a conversion table", and Mark's defining problem is an excess of unassessed reading, not a shortage of it (`avatar-mark.md` §A, "read enough to be dangerous and not enough to be sure"). The retest-and-trend section was rejected because its ask is "come back in six weeks", which is a longer loop than a man holding a flagged sheet tonight is in. This shape asks him to do one thing with a sheet he already owns: recall the week the sample was taken. Both alternatives clear compliance identically, so avatar fit was the only live axis.
- **Distance from the two existing derivatives of this article, named rather than assumed.** `2026-07-31-four-things-on-the-sheet` (LinkedIn) enters through the chatbot behaviour and wedges on the reference range answering a different question. `2026-08-14-carousel-how-to-read-blood-test-results` (Instagram) runs the whole article as a six-idea deck. This one enters through a single flagged line on a printout, and its wedge is that one out-of-range value on one day is a prompt rather than a label. The 19-in-20 figure appears in both this and the LinkedIn post, and it is doing different work: there it argues the range answers the wrong question, here it argues a healthy man outside the band is expected by design. The two-questions reframe is deliberately absent from this post so the shapes do not converge.
- **The timing angle was available and is already owned.** `2026-07-31-what-time-was-it-taken` runs the morning-sampling rule as a short-form script. It is the strongest single idea left in this article and it is spoken for, so it is referenced here only as one item inside the noise list ("the time the blood was drawn") and never developed.
- **The GP boundary is load-bearing, not a disclaimer, and its POSITION was set by measurement.** A post arguing that a flagged number is often noise is one careless paragraph away from reading as "ignore your abnormal result", so the escalation lines are carried in the article's own terms. The first draft put them seventh, at character 937 of a 1,594-character body. Facebook's "See more" cut falls around 400 to 480 characters, so every reassuring line was visible without a click and every escalation line was behind one. The pre-flight measured it and the paragraph was moved to second, where it now runs 95 to 397 and closes inside the tightest plausible fold. **The visible half of this post is now the half that routes onward, and the reassurance is the part you have to click for**, which is the right way round for health copy on a cold feed. Nothing in the copy was softened to achieve it: the change was to the running order alone, and the delta scan confirms zero findings introduced and zero removed.
- **"Urgently" was restored while moving it.** The first draft read "goes to your GP whatever the number says"; the article's own heading reads "Go to your GP urgently, whatever the number". A derivative may claim less than its source, but not in the escalation direction, which is the one place where claiming less is the unsafe way to be wrong.
- **Device 7 (understatement at the peak):** "Two things don't wait." and "That's the urgent list, and it's short." The two shortest lines in the post, both carrying the weight, both in the plainest possible words. The second doubles as the pivot out of the escalation, so the post can relax without anyone saying "but don't worry".
- **Close rotated deliberately.** Measured across the asset library on 2026-08-17: 6 of the 14 bodied assets close on a question and 4 of those 6 arrive at it through an `If you have / If you are` conditional, and two of the link closes reuse "If you are not sure which check makes sense" almost verbatim. The question is kept (it is the platform mechanic) and the route to it is changed: it is hung off the last concrete detail, in the second person, with no conditional. The link line then arrives on its own sentence rather than as the question's clause. Opener checked against the same library: no asset opens on "One line", and the two converging openers there (`Most men…` and `If you are…`) are both avoided.
- **No personal history, no bloodwork figure, and nothing written as Mark.** There is no first person in the post at all, which is correct for a brand page. The only figures are the 19-in-20 and 1-in-20 pair, both quoted from the article.
- **`cta: quiz` matches the Facebook format**, which routes to the router rather than to the article. Full `https://` scheme used. `written-post-playbook.md` records the scheme rule as ruled for LinkedIn and explicitly **not yet ruled for Facebook**; full scheme is the safer default here and stays flagged below rather than recorded as settled.
- **`thumb: none`, per Keith's 2026-08-05 ruling** recorded in `2026-08-04-put-it-down-to-age.md`: a Facebook post does not need a bespoke cover, and the image attached at scheduling is the linked article's own `imgSrc`. This diverges from the `/script` Step 5 table, which still says 1200x630; logged as observation 298.

## Rails held

Written as an allowlist of what the copy does, never a list of what it avoids (Observation 83).

The post stays on the education side of the line throughout. It describes what a single measurement is, lists ordinary everyday things that move a marker, and states that a value outside the band is a reason to look again. It quotes two figures, the 19-in-20 coverage and the 1-in-20 remainder, both taken from the article and neither belonging to any person. It carries the article's own escalation lines in the body: a lab-flagged urgent result follows the lab or NHS 111, and red-flag symptoms go to the GP whatever the number says. Its corrective energy is pointed at how a single sheet gets read, and it says outright that a doctor reads a result inside a wider picture, which credits clinical practice rather than faulting it. It names no marker, no ingredient and no product, so the EFSA tables are not in play and the Kit 1 scoping rule is not engaged. It carries no personal result, so there is nothing to substantiate against a filed number. The single CTA is a soft in-post link to the test selector, which the funnel map allows at MOFU. No em dashes, no bullet lists in the post body, no engagement bait.
